deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. Folio 12 is a set of German lecture or reading notes on ancient history, from a section headed 'IV. Phönizier' (Phoenicians) that begins on the previous page. Its content and order match the standard Göttingen ancient-history curriculum of the period, in particular A. H. L. Heeren's treatment of the trade and politics of ancient peoples. The page says the following.
(a) The Phoenicians were probably Arabs. From the earliest times they lived in (or ruled) cities, each with its own territory, so the cities were independent of one another. Like the Jews, they were already somewhat cultivated.
(b) Under the heading 'Allgemeine Bemerkungen' (general remarks) there are three numbered points:
1. The Phoenician cities formed a number of small states. They were colonies of one another, so they made alliances among themselves.
2. Although formally independent, some cities grew more powerful than others, and a kind of hegemony ('Oberherrschaft') arose.
3. The internal constitutions of the cities seem to have been fairly similar. Each had a king, but the constitution came close to the aristocratic type.
(c) Under the heading 'Geschichte von Sidon' (history of Sidon): Sidon was the oldest city. It appears from that time on as the most flourishing city of Phoenicia and stayed so, the sentence continuing on the next page, until Tyre eclipsed it.
No formulas, computations, derivations or figures appear. The hand and the subject suggest a student's or another person's history notebook bound into the bundle, not Gauss's own mathematical work. The bundle label 'Lagrange1816' does not match the content, so this folio may be a binding or archival miscellany. That is an inference, not a certainty.
errors: No mathematical content, so there are no mathematical errors. On the historical side, the claims (Phoenicians as Arabs, Sidon as the oldest city, the cities' aristocratic-monarchic constitutions) reflect early-19th-century textbook views, for example Heeren's. Modern scholarship would not accept the 'Arab' origin claim as stated.
